summary: This work develops a real-time logical error rate (LER) predictor for surface code QEC by correlating detector fire rate (DFR)—readily available from stabilizer measurements—with LER using circuits simulated with physical error rates from real hardware. The approach pairs this predictor with a dynamic remapping scheme that relocates drifted logical qubits to fresh tiles while their original tiles undergo recalibration, demonstrating effective drift mitigation for small code distances.
motivation: Real quantum hardware exhibits temporally-varying noise that violates standard QEC assumptions of spatially-uniform and temporally-constant error rates, yet characterizing true error rates mid-execution is infeasible, requiring methods to detect and respond to drift without additional characterization overhead.
method: A DFR-to-LER predictor is trained using Stim simulations spanning physical error rates from IBM and Google hardware traces, establishing the scaling $p_L \propto (\mathrm{DFR})^{(d+1)/2}$ across code distances. The predictor uses a tunable buffer of recent DFRs and confidence parameter $\alpha$ to produce conservative LER estimates; when predicted LER exceeds a threshold, a remap operation moves the logical qubit to a dedicated relocation patch while the original tile is recalibrated.
result: The DFR-based predictor achieves accurate real-time LER predictions without additional sampling overhead, and remapping maintains target LER with a relocation-qubit ratio $M/N \leq 1$ for small distances; however, spatial efficiency diminishes as $d^{-2}$, making remapping preferable only for $d \lesssim 5$ compared to code deformation methods for larger codes.
